coherence.reasons: Both lead with the same answer and support it with market, economics, funding and alternative sections. X is tighter: slide 3 sets out six conditions the founders' hypothesis needs, and each later section tests one of them, so governing thought, summary, titles and evidence line up one-to-one. Y's hierarchy is also sound, with section summary slides and action titles, but it is more diffuse. Its third pillar mixes pop-up density, loyalty and an extrapolated acquisition bill, and its executive-summary sub-points are single illustrative facts rather than the full support for each claim. X's options table and cash model also tie the recommendation directly to the two board constraints.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred conclusion: do not launch, grow software, sell store-based fast delivery to grocers, with re-entry triggers. X weighs the alternatives better. It constructs and quantifies the one-store pilot (the tempting middle option) and rejects it because the median store loses $6.17 per order, the runway rule is breached in month 10 and it adds little learning. It also finds the minimum software growth rate (34%) that keeps the runway rule, phases hires against signed contracts and sets a 90-day checkpoint. Its re-entry triggers include the fee route that Zipcart showed. Y compares only launch against software and never addresses a pilot or capped test. Its treatment of the channel conflict with grocers (a commitment not to operate in customers' cities) is a good addition, and it flags that the software path depends on growth holding, but with only a 30% data point. X's trade-off work is more complete.

evidence.reasons: Both get the core calculations right: −$6.17, −$1.76, −$12.57, +$2.02, $2.5M and about 6 months of runway, −$1.05 with Zipcart's moves, and break-even ARR of about $11M. X gives the CAGR of 41.5% explicitly; Y gives year-on-year rates and 'more than 40% on average'. X adds a monthly cash model under both readings of the $9.5M, a payback table by scenario, the break-even density with Zipcart's moves (about 1,042 orders a day) and a sanity check that the plan implies $266M of sales, more than QuickBasket's revenue. X has one small error: the density and promotions values in the one-driver sensitivity are swapped (+0.22 and +0.27), which does not affect the conclusion. Y adds correct and useful figures: −$0.48 with no volume loss, 14.4 orders per rider-hour to break even, and the $7.1 an hour rider-pay break-even. Its $13.7M 'cost to fill nine stores' is arithmetically right but a heavy extrapolation, and the headline 'density cannot be bought' is stronger than that supports. Y's statement that Zipcart's turnaround owed nothing to density overlooks that it was Zipcart's densest city. X uses the Zipcart evidence more accurately.

revision.reasons: Both reject the founders' hypothesis, as the evidence requires, and both concede that the growth claim is true. X handles it more explicitly and more fairly. It states the hypothesis, breaks it into six testable conditions and gives a verdict on each. It grants the caveat that the pop-up was early (six weeks, ramping from about 179 to 408 orders a day) and then shows that ramp-up alone still leaves −$6.17 at the median. It also accepts that the Zipcart evidence shows a profitable route may exist at top-quartile density with premium pricing, and builds that into a re-entry trigger. Y rejects the hypothesis soundly and tests the 'nobody owns the Midwest' and 'it can be done' claims, but it treats the Zipcart case mainly as a price rise and does not acknowledge the density level at which the economics would turn positive.

overall.reasons: Both documents would lead the board to the right decision with correct core numbers. X serves the board better. It tests the founders' case condition by condition, quantifies and rejects the pilot compromise the founders are likely to propose next, and models cash month by month for each option under both readings of the $9.5M. It gives the software path an explicit growth threshold (34%) with phased hiring and a 90-day checkpoint, and it engages with the Zipcart counter-evidence in a balanced way. Y is accurate and has some good additions (rider-pay sensitivity, the no-volume-loss Zipcart case, the channel-conflict commitment), but it is longer, omits the pilot option and leans on a more speculative acquisition-cost extrapolation.
